source.title: Reservoir Computing as a Language Model

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the supplied text includes the main paper and appendix.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures language-model cross-entropy across parameter sizes, testing the size–loss relationship with small character-level models and a reservoir architecture rather than reproducing the original scaling-law setup.
record.gate_note: The study reports held-out test-loss curves for three architecture families across model sizes, and explicitly gives the best test loss for each family. It also reports fits of best training loss against parameter count for OpenWebText models. It does not report extrapolation from small runs, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or downstream-task predictability. Training-loss fits are not held-out-loss results.
record.test_reason: The study fits minimum loss against trainable parameter count for transformer and layered-reservoir (LAERC) language models on OpenWebText (Fig. 7, Eq. 9), citing Kaplan et al. This is a new architecture setting with a result on V1. The character-level Shakespeare sweep also varies model size, but only figure curves and unattributed minima are reported. It is a weak test: about one decade of parameters, a log-linear fit form, and a Fig. 7 caption that says training loss while the axis says testing loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors say transformers achieve the best loss and reservoirs are far cheaper and competitive, and that layered reservoirs follow a 'power-law trend' with parameters, numerically weaker than transformers. Correction: the paper's Fig. 7 axis is labelled 'Best Testing loss' while its caption says training loss, so the record should not assert training loss unambiguously.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a 9-million-character Shakespeare corpus for held-out character-level evaluation across roughly 15000–155000 trainable parameters, and separately fits best training loss against parameter count for OpenWebText models. It does not use the original scaling-law study's broad parameter, data, and compute sweeps or test small-run extrapolation.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports different scaling slopes for transformer and LAERC architectures; it notes that reservoir parameterization, coupling topology, and training protocol were not exhaustively tuned, but does not measure the effect of changing those choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Fitted loss-vs-parameter slope differs about twofold between transformers and fixed-reservoir LAERC models trained with the same hyperparameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The size-scaling slope of language-model loss depends on architecture family (e.g. fixed reservoirs replacing attention scale more weakly).

fits_no_version.finding: Training/inference time scales with trainable parameters much more slowly for reservoir models (Fig. 4 log fits).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute cost versus parameter count differs by architecture (not a loss scaling law).

record.problems: The held-out character-level size sweep spans only about one order of magnitude, and the text supplies no configuration-specific numerical test losses or uncertainty estimates. The OpenWebText scaling fit uses best training loss rather than held-out loss. The AERC parameter count for its largest configuration differs between Table I and the Fig. 2 legend.

untested.parts: Several orders of magnitude (only about one decade in each sweep); scaling in tokens or compute; confirming the bottleneck condition; a clearly held-out loss in the OpenWebText fit; a true power-law functional fit.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No fixed-compute allocation of parameters vs tokens.
No fixed-parameter shape comparison; transformer configurations change width, depth and heads together with size.
Text only; no other modality, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer regime.
No downstream tasks. N-gram overlap of generated text versus size (Fig. 3) is not a downstream-task measure.
No comparison of fitting choices; the different slopes reflect architecture, not fitting setup.

missing.what: Per-configuration best loss values (eight models, four per family) behind the Fig. 7 fits, plus clarification of whether they are training or held-out loss (caption and axis label conflict).
Whether held-out test loss decreases monotonically with size within each Shakespeare family; the text says only that loss variance across sizes is larger for RC/AERC.
missing.locator: Fig. 2 bottom row; Sec. III A

record.verdict_notes: The paper's fitted form L = a·log10 N + b is logarithmic, not a power law; over one decade the two are hard to distinguish. The authors attribute the steep transformer slope to the small-parameter regime. The scaling evidence is a side result of an architecture paper. The V1 verdicts are weak and confined to about 10^6–10^7 parameters. No uncertainty estimates and no repeated seeds are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The held-out test-loss sweep varies parameter count only, over approximately 15,000–155,000 trainable parameters; it does not test several orders of magnitude or independently vary tokens and compute while the other factors are not bottlenecks.
No prediction of larger-run losses from fits to smaller runs.
No fixed-compute-budget comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.

The study compares different architecture families and sweeps configurations, but does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count to test whether their effects are small.
The study uses text data and different language-model architectures; it does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study does not test how fitting choices affect exponents or allocation trends, or whether curves bend away from a single power law.
